label: DevOps
description: Delivery-stack MCQ: Docker & Kubernetes, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Redis and the CI/CD pipelines that glue them together.

questions.title: What does `docker run -d nginx` do differently from `docker run nginx`?
questions.prompt: What does `docker run -d nginx` do differently from `docker run nginx`?

options.text: It runs nginx with an interactive terminal attached
It runs nginx detached in the background so the shell returns immediately
It rebuilds the image before running

questions.explanation: The `-d` flag runs the container detached. Without it the container's logs stream into the terminal and the shell stays attached until the container exits.

questions.title: A Dockerfile line reads `COPY package.json ./`. When does that layer rebuild?
questions.prompt: A Dockerfile line reads `COPY package.json ./`. When does that layer rebuild?

options.text: Only when package.json or the build context changes — otherwise the cached layer is reused
Only when the image tag changes
Whenever the base image is pulled

questions.explanation: Docker caches layers in order, so copying the manifest before the source keeps the expensive install layer valid while only application code changes.

questions.title: Which command shows only the containers currently running?
questions.prompt: Which command shows only the containers currently running?
questions.explanation: `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker ps -a` also includes stopped ones. `docker images` lists images, not containers.

questions.title: In a Dockerfile, what is the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`?
questions.prompt: In a Dockerfile, what is the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`?

options.text: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable while CMD supplies default arguments that can be overridden at run time
CMD runs at build time and ENTRYPOINT at run time
ENTRYPOINT only works on Windows images

questions.explanation: `ENTRYPOINT` pins the executable; `CMD` provides defaults that `docker run <image> <args>` can override on the command line.

questions.title: What problem does `docker compose up` solve?
questions.prompt: What problem does `docker compose up` solve?

options.text: It compiles Go binaries for containers
It starts every service in a compose file (app, database, cache) with one command

questions.explanation: Compose reads a declarative compose.yaml and brings the whole multi-container stack up together with shared networking.

questions.title: An image is 1.4 GB and CI bandwidth is the bottleneck. Which change shrinks it most?
questions.prompt: An image is 1.4 GB and CI bandwidth is the bottleneck. Which change shrinks it most?

options.text: Switch the final stage to a slim/distroless base and use a multi-stage build
Run apt-get upgrade in the final stage

questions.explanation: Most bytes come from the base image and build-only tooling. A multi-stage build copies just the artifact into a minimal runtime image.

questions.title: A container must reach another service in the same compose file. How does it address it?
questions.prompt: A container must reach another service in the same compose file. How does it address it?

options.text: By the service name from compose.yaml, which Compose registers as a DNS name
By localhost of the host machine

questions.explanation: Compose creates a user-defined network and registers each service under its service name, so `postgres:5432` just works.

questions.title: Why does a `RUN rm -rf /var/cache` line NOT shrink the final image?
questions.prompt: Why does a `RUN rm -rf /var/cache` line NOT shrink the final image?

options.text: rm is unavailable during docker build
Each instruction is a layer — the deleted bytes remain in the earlier layer

questions.explanation: Layers are additive; deleting later only hides the bytes. Clean up inside the same RUN, or discard the whole layer with a multi-stage build.

questions.title: What does the `HEALTHCHECK` instruction do for a container?
questions.prompt: What does the `HEALTHCHECK` instruction do for a container?

options.text: Reports build status to Docker Hub
Runs a periodic command and marks the container healthy or unhealthy so orchestrators can route around failures
Auto-restarts the container when it exits

questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK lets the runtime probe the process. Compose uses it for `service_healthy` dependencies, and Kubernetes covers the same ground with its own probes.

questions.title: Which build flag forces every Dockerfile instruction to re-run?
questions.prompt: Which build flag forces every Dockerfile instruction to re-run?
questions.explanation: `docker build --no-cache` bypasses the layer cache, the standard fix when a stale cache produces a broken image.

questions.title: Where should a production API key live so it never bakes into an image layer?
questions.prompt: Where should a production API key live so it never bakes into an image layer?

options.text: As an ARG in the Dockerfile
As an ENV set at build time
Injected at run time via a secret, env var or the orchestrator's secret store

questions.explanation: Anything written at build time (ARG, ENV, COPY) persists in image history. Secrets belong to the run-time environment.

questions.title: Which construct most reliably waits for postgres before starting the app in compose?
questions.prompt: Which construct most reliably waits for postgres before starting the app in compose?

options.text: A healthcheck plus depends_on: condition: service_healthy

questions.explanation: Plain depends_on only orders container creation, not readiness. The healthcheck condition waits until postgres actually accepts connections.

questions.title: In CI the npm dependency layer rebuilds although package.json is unchanged. Most likely cause?
questions.prompt: In CI the npm dependency layer rebuilds although package.json is unchanged. Most likely cause?

options.text: package-lock.json is copied later than package.json, so the cache invalidates at that instruction
Docker cache is disabled for node images

questions.explanation: Cache invalidates at the first changed instruction. Copy both manifest files (and nothing else) before running the install so the layer stays hot.

questions.title: What does `docker compose up --scale api=3` actually give you?
questions.prompt: What does `docker compose up --scale api=3` actually give you?

options.text: Three separate networks, one per replica
Three replicas sharing the service DNS name so queries round-robin across them

questions.explanation: Scaling in Compose creates more containers for the service; they all register under the same DNS name, giving simple load balancing.

questions.title: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
questions.prompt: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
questions.explanation: A pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace and volumes; deployments and services operate *on* pods.

questions.title: Which resource exposes a set of pods to traffic inside the cluster?
questions.prompt: Which resource exposes a set of pods to traffic inside the cluster?
questions.explanation: A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of pods, which are ephemeral and get new IPs whenever they restart.

questions.title: What does `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` do?
questions.prompt: What does `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` do?

options.text: Rolls the deployment back to its previous revision

questions.explanation: Rollout undo reverts to the last recorded ReplicaSet revision — the fastest recovery from a bad release.

questions.title: A pod's liveness probe fails ~40 seconds after start. What should be configured?
questions.prompt: A pod's liveness probe fails ~40 seconds after start. What should be configured?

options.text: initialDelaySeconds so the probe waits until the application finishes booting

questions.explanation: Liveness probes firing before boot completes cause restart loops. initialDelaySeconds (or a startupProbe) covers slow starts; readiness decides when traffic is sent.

questions.title: Which object holds non-sensitive configuration the pod reads as environment variables?
questions.prompt: Which object holds non-sensitive configuration the pod reads as environment variables?
questions.explanation: ConfigMaps carry configuration, mounted as files or injected via envFrom. Secrets are the counterpart for credentials.

questions.title: How do you keep three replicas off the same node?
questions.prompt: How do you keep three replicas off the same node?
questions.explanation: Anti-affinity makes the scheduler spread replicas across nodes — required or preferred depending on how strictly the HA policy must hold.

questions.title: What does a `readinessProbe` control?
questions.prompt: What does a `readinessProbe` control?

options.text: How long the container may run
Whether the pod is added to the Service endpoints and receives traffic

questions.explanation: Readiness gates traffic: failing pods are removed from Service endpoints while the container keeps running and the liveness probe keeps it alive.

questions.title: A Deployment sets maxUnavailable=0, maxSurge=100%. What happens on a bad release?
questions.prompt: A Deployment sets maxUnavailable=0, maxSurge=100%. What happens on a bad release?

options.text: A replacement pod starts before any old pod is removed, so capacity is preserved while the rollout proceeds
The API server rejects the rollout

questions.explanation: maxSurge starts the new pod first and maxUnavailable=0 keeps old replicas serving; the swap happens only when the new pod is ready.

questions.title: On what does a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler base its decisions by default?
questions.prompt: On what does a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler base its decisions by default?

options.text: Average pod CPU utilisation against a configured target

questions.explanation: HPA computes average pod CPU (other metrics require the custom-metrics adapter) and adjusts replicas to hit the target utilisation.

questions.title: Why is a hostPath volume usually discouraged for shared application data?
questions.prompt: Why is a hostPath volume usually discouraged for shared application data?

options.text: Data is tied to one node — it disappears if the pod is rescheduled elsewhere and exposes the node's files

questions.explanation: hostPath is node-local and leaks host paths into containers. A PVC backed by a proper StorageClass is the portable, durable answer.

questions.title: What is the closest MongoDB analogue of a SQL table?
questions.prompt: What is the closest MongoDB analogue of a SQL table?
questions.explanation: Collections group documents; a single BSON document plays the role a row plays in SQL.

questions.title: Which field is indexed automatically on every collection?
questions.prompt: Which field is indexed automatically on every collection?

options.text: None — indexes are always created manually

questions.explanation: MongoDB auto-creates a unique index on `_id`, guaranteeing a fast primary lookup for every document.

questions.title: By default, what happens when you iterate a large `find()` cursor?
questions.prompt: By default, what happens when you iterate a large `find()` cursor?

options.text: Every match is loaded into memory immediately
Documents stream in batches, so huge result sets can be processed without buffering them
Only the first document is returned
The query blocks until it times out

questions.explanation: Cursors fetch batches (101 documents by default), which keeps memory bounded while you iterate.

questions.title: Orders must be grouped by status and summed by amount. Which aggregation pair does that?
questions.prompt: Orders must be grouped by status and summed by amount. Which aggregation pair does that?
questions.explanation: `$match` filters early so indexes apply, and `$group` performs the grouping and summation — `$group` is the aggregating stage.

questions.title: Why does `db.users.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { name: "Ann" })` fail?
questions.prompt: Why does `db.users.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { name: "Ann" })` fail?

options.text: The update document must use operators such as $set — a bare document is treated as a replacement

questions.explanation: Replacement documents are only valid with `replaceOne`. `updateOne` requires update operators like `$set` or `$inc`.

questions.title: Which index best supports `find({ status: 1 }).sort({ createdAt: -1 })`?
questions.prompt: Which index best supports `find({ status: 1 }).sort({ createdAt: -1 })`?
questions.explanation: The equality prefix plus descending sort index returns results already in order, avoiding MongoDB's 32 MB in-memory sort limit.

questions.title: How do `primaryPreferred` and `secondary` read preferences differ?
questions.prompt: How do `primaryPreferred` and `secondary` read preferences differ?

options.text: secondary always reads replicas (possibly stale); primaryPreferred prefers the primary and falls back to replicas

questions.explanation: secondary spreads read load but may serve stale data; primaryPreferred only touches replicas when the primary is unavailable.

questions.title: What does write concern `w: majority` guarantee?
questions.prompt: What does write concern `w: majority` guarantee?

options.text: The write is acknowledged after a majority of voting nodes have persisted it, so it survives a later failover

questions.explanation: majority waits until more than half the voting set has the write — a deliberate durability-over-latency trade.

questions.title: A single document hits the 16 MB cap because every order item is embedded. What is the fix?
questions.prompt: A single document hits the 16 MB cap because every order item is embedded. What is the fix?

options.text: Raise the limit with a config flag
Move items into a child collection and reference them from the parent

questions.explanation: 16 MB is a hard BSON limit; unbounded one-to-many data belongs in its own collection keyed by the parent id.

questions.title: Why do inserts skew onto one shard after sharding on a monotonically increasing _id?
questions.prompt: Why do inserts skew onto one shard after sharding on a monotonically increasing _id?

options.text: New keys always land in the last chunk, concentrating writes instead of spreading them

questions.explanation: Rising keys funnel every insert into the newest chunk; a hashed or otherwise randomised shard key spreads the load.

questions.title: Which clause filters rows *before* GROUP BY runs?
questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows *before* GROUP BY runs?
questions.explanation: `WHERE` filters individual rows before aggregation; `HAVING` filters the aggregated groups afterwards.

questions.title: What does `a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.id` return?
questions.prompt: What does `a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.id` return?

options.text: Only rows where the condition matches on both sides

questions.explanation: An inner join keeps matching pairs only; unmatched rows from either side are dropped (a FULL OUTER JOIN would keep them).

questions.title: Which keyword locks the rows a SELECT reads until the transaction ends?
questions.prompt: Which keyword locks the rows a SELECT reads until the transaction ends?
questions.explanation: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row-locks the result so concurrent writers wait — the standard defence against lost updates.

questions.title: What is the difference between CHAR(n) and VARCHAR(n) for a name column?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between CHAR(n) and VARCHAR(n) for a name column?

options.text: CHAR pads with spaces to the fixed length, VARCHAR stores only the actual characters
CHAR supports Unicode, VARCHAR does not

questions.explanation: CHAR(n) space-pads to exactly n characters, which surprises equality checks; VARCHAR(n) stores only what you insert.

questions.title: Why can `WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@x.com'` skip a plain index on email?
questions.prompt: Why can `WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@x.com'` skip a plain index on email?

options.text: Function calls are banned in WHERE
The predicate is an expression while the index covers the raw column — index lower(email) instead
PostgreSQL cannot index functions at all

questions.explanation: An index scan must match the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` lets the planner use it.

questions.title: What does VACUUM accomplish that DELETE alone does not?
questions.prompt: What does VACUUM accomplish that DELETE alone does not?

options.text: Reclaims dead tuples, refreshes visibility maps and prevents transaction ID wraparound

questions.explanation: DELETE only marks rows dead; vacuum reclaims space, updates statistics and enables index-only scans via the visibility map.

questions.title: Which tool reveals that a correlated subquery runs once per outer row?
questions.prompt: Which tool reveals that a correlated subquery runs once per outer row?
questions.explanation: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query and reports loops per plan node, exposing a nested loop whose inner query executes N times.

questions.title: A query returns rows in a different order on each run. Which clause makes it deterministic?
questions.prompt: A query returns rows in a different order on each run. Which clause makes it deterministic?
questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY the plan is free to return parallel or hash order; ORDER BY pins the sequence.

questions.title: A yearly DELETE on a 200M-row table runs for minutes and bloats the table. Best fix?
questions.prompt: A yearly DELETE on a 200M-row table runs for minutes and bloats the table. Best fix?

options.text: Delete in small batches so locks stay short and autovacuum can reclaim incrementally
Wrap it in one long transaction

questions.explanation: Batched deletes keep lock times and WAL bursts small and let vacuum keep up instead of producing one giant dead-tuple spike.

questions.title: Which index type suits append-ordered time-series ranges and stays tiny?
questions.prompt: Which index type suits append-ordered time-series ranges and stays tiny?
questions.explanation: BRIN stores min/max per block range, so for naturally ordered data like timestamps it is orders of magnitude smaller than a B-tree.

questions.title: Why is Redis usually faster than a relational database?
questions.prompt: Why is Redis usually faster than a relational database?

options.text: The dataset lives in memory and commands run in a single event loop without lock contention
It stores data on SSD only

questions.explanation: In-memory storage plus a single-threaded command loop means no lock contention between clients — the source of Redis's latency.

questions.title: Which structure fits a leaderboard ordered by score?
questions.prompt: Which structure fits a leaderboard ordered by score?
questions.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score, giving O(log N) rank and range queries — exactly what a leaderboard needs.

questions.title: Which command performs an atomic increment?
questions.prompt: Which command performs an atomic increment?
questions.explanation: `INCR` is atomic, creates the key when missing, and is the building block for counters and rate limits.

questions.title: How do you give a key a 60-second lifetime?
questions.prompt: How do you give a key a 60-second lifetime?
questions.explanation: `EXPIRE key 60` sets a TTL in seconds; `SET key v EX 60` does it in one atomic command.

questions.title: What is the difference between RDB and AOF persistence?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between RDB and AOF persistence?

options.text: RDB takes periodic snapshots while AOF appends writes — AOF loses less data but grows larger

questions.explanation: RDB gives compact point-in-time snapshots; AOF replays an append log (fsync everysec by default) trading size for durability.

questions.title: How does Redis Cluster route a key?
questions.prompt: How does Redis Cluster route a key?

options.text: CRC16(key) mod 16384 mapped through hash-slot ownership

questions.explanation: CRC16(key) % 16384 picks one of 16384 hash slots, and each slot lives on exactly one primary — node moves keep slots stable.

questions.title: What problem does `SET mylock <token> NX PX 5000` solve?
questions.prompt: What problem does `SET mylock <token> NX PX 5000` solve?

options.text: It caches five keys at once
It creates a lock that expires after 5 seconds if the holder crashes
It replicates the key to five nodes

questions.explanation: NX makes the set only-if-absent (one winner) and PX bounds the lock so a dead holder can never block others forever.

questions.title: Which distributed-lock release pattern is safe?
questions.prompt: Which distributed-lock release pattern is safe?

options.text: Read the token, then release only when it still matches (compare-and-delete, ideally as a Lua script)

questions.explanation: Between an owner's check and delete, the lock may have expired and been re-acquired; the token check (atomically in Lua) prevents deleting someone else's lock.

questions.title: maxmemory is reached with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. What happens on the next write?
questions.prompt: maxmemory is reached with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. What happens on the next write?

options.text: Writes fail with OOM errors until memory is freed or a policy is configured

questions.explanation: noeviction keeps every key and refuses new writes once full — an outage unless you configure an LRU/LFU policy or add capacity.
